Simulate a toy dataset of unlinked loci

Source: R/gt_simulate_bn.R
gt_simulate_bn.Rd

Simulates the genotypes of a few populations at unlinked biallelic loci under the Balding-Nichols model, and returns them as a gen_tibble. This is a toy simulator for quick checks of methods on unlinked loci (e.g. that a PCA separates populations, or how a statistic behaves with missing genotypes); it is not meant for inference.

Usage

gt_simulate_bn(
  n_indiv = 20,
  n_loci = 1000,
  fst = 0.05,
  missing = 0,
  freq_range = c(0.05, 0.95),
  backingfile = NULL
)

Arguments

n_indiv

the number of individuals per population: one value, or one per population.

n_loci

the number of loci.

fst

the divergence (\(F_{ST}\)) of each population from the ancestral population: one value, or one per population. The number of populations is the longer of n_indiv and fst.

missing

the probability that a genotype is missing: one value, or one per individual (e.g. to give individuals different missingness).

freq_range

the range of the (uniform) distribution of the ancestral allele frequencies.

backingfile

the path, without extension, of the backing files; by default a temporary file.

Value

a gen_tibble with columns id, population and genotypes.

Details

Each locus has an ancestral allele frequency \(p\) drawn uniformly in freq_range. The frequency in population \(k\) is drawn from a beta distribution with mean \(p\) and variance \(F_k p (1-p)\) (the Balding-Nichols model, i.e. independent drift of each population from a common ancestor, a star-shaped tree), and the genotypes of its individuals are binomial draws of two alleles at that frequency (Hardy-Weinberg proportions). Genotypes are then set to missing at random with probability missing.

The model has no linkage, mutation, recombination, demographic history or tree of populations: for realistic data, simulate with the coalescent (e.g. msprime, which can be run from R with the slendr package).

All loci are placed on chromosome 1, 1,000 bp apart, but they are independent. Some loci can be monomorphic in the sample. The genotypes are generated in memory before being written to the backing file, so keep the datasets small. Use set.seed() beforehand for reproducible datasets.

References

Balding D.J. and Nichols R.A. (1995) A method for quantifying differentiation between populations at multi-allelic loci and its implications for investigating identity and paternity. Genetica 96: 3-12.

Baumdicker F. et al. (2022) Efficient ancestry and mutation simulation with msprime 1.0. Genetics 220: iyab229.

Petr M., Haller B.C., Ralph P.L. and Racimo F. (2023) slendr: a framework for spatio-temporal population genomic simulations on geographic landscapes. Peer Community Journal 3: e121.

Examples

set.seed(1)
# three populations of 20 individuals, 500 loci
sim_gt <- gt_simulate_bn(
  n_indiv = 20, n_loci = 500, fst = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1)
)
sim_gt
#> # A gen_tibble: 500 loci
#> # A tibble:     60 × 3
#>    id    population  genotypes
#>    <chr> <chr>      <vctr_SNP>
#>  1 ind1  pop1        [1,1,...]
#>  2 ind2  pop1        [0,0,...]
#>  3 ind3  pop1        [1,1,...]
#>  4 ind4  pop1        [0,1,...]
#>  5 ind5  pop1        [0,0,...]
#>  6 ind6  pop1        [1,1,...]
#>  7 ind7  pop1        [1,0,...]
#>  8 ind8  pop1        [0,0,...]
#>  9 ind9  pop1        [0,1,...]
#> 10 ind10 pop1        [1,0,...]
#> # ℹ 50 more rows
# three populations with missing genotypes, increasing from 0 to 90%
# across the individuals of each population
sim_missing <- gt_simulate_bn(
  n_indiv = c(20, 20, 20), n_loci = 500, fst = 0.05,
  missing = rep(seq(0, 0.9, length.out = 20), 3)
)
